text:
Transcript: COL-2026-07-03 12:31:19
[00:02 - 01:00] Speaker 1: We weren’t a hundred feet down the road when Jane said, “There should be dead people everywhere. That’s what the traffic’s like in Naples, Italy. Cars bumper to bumper, side by side, Sometimes four and five lanes deep with scooters dodging in and out between the cars. And the scooters don’t just have one person on them. ;, they usually have often have one person.” Plus another person or one person plus, one kid and another kid standing in front of the driver. It’s absolutely chaotic and rather insane. We both wondered, what we’d gotten ourselves into. That’s how we started our time in Naples, And it took about a day or so before when we were in a cab, we could keep our eyes open because when the roads aren’t wide and crowded, the roads are more like narrow streets. Booking Strategy

When to Book
Timeline: - 2-3 months ahead: Best balance of price and availability - Too early: Prices often haven’t dropped to competitive levels - Too late: Limited availability, higher prices
For a June departure: Book by late March/early April


Booking Checklist

Compare prices on Google Flights, airline sites, and SkyLux

Select seats early (aisle vs. window preference)
Add to calendar with confirmation numbers

Seat Selection Tips
Transatlantic Leg: - Business/First: Window for sleep, aisle for movement - Economy: Aisle for long-haul comfort and bathroom access - Avoid seats near lavatories and galleys (noise) - Emergency exit rows: More legroom but no under-seat storage during takeoff/landing
European Connection: - Usually shorter flights (1-2 hours) - Less critical but still book early for best selection

Why Intercity (IC) is the right choice: - Runs the full Naples → Brindisi route without changing trains - Makes major stops only (Foggia, Bari, coastal towns) — not every tiny station - First Class on IC trains: reserved seat, more space, dedicated car, quieter - IC trains are not Frecciarossa-class but they are proper express trains - Fares: €15–40 First Class depending on advance booking - Book at trenitalia.com — search Naples Centrale → Brindisi, filter by IC
What makes the “milk run” concern valid: The Bari→Brindisi regional (Regionale) connection, if you take the Frecciarossa-then-change-at-Bari approach, IS slow — it stops at many coastal towns. That’s the connection to avoid. The IC bypasses this entirely.
Booking tip: IC trains must be booked on Trenitalia (Italo doesn’t serve this southern route). Book 2–4 weeks ahead for best fares and seat selection.


Understanding Puglia Geography
Important: Brindisi is IN Puglia, not before it. The train journey IS a tour through Puglia:
Route Path (North to South): 1. Caserta - Royal Palace (Reggia di Caserta), visible from station 2. Benevento - Roman Arch of Trajan 3. Foggia - Enter Puglia here (gateway to Gargano Peninsula) 4. Bari - Puglia’s capital (~3.5h from Naples) 5. Polignano a Mare - Dramatic cliffside town 6. Ostuni - “White City” on hilltop 7. Brindisi - Historic port city (~5.5h from Naples) 8. Lecce - “Florence of the South” (~6h from Naples, 30 min beyond Brindisi)


Recommended Train
Intercity (IC) Naples Centrale → Brindisi - Morning departure recommended (arrive Brindisi early afternoon) - Check current schedules at trenitalia.com — schedules change seasonally - First Class car: look for “Prima Classe” designation when booking - Journey time: approximately 5h 30min direct
Departure Times: - Morning Options: Earliest ~8:12 AM, Latest ~6:12 PM - Strategy: Take morning train to maximize daylight views through Puglia


Scenic Journey Highlights
What You’ll See: - Crossing the Apennines (mountains) - Entering the Tavoliere delle Puglie (plains) - Adriatic coastline (sit on LEFT side after Foggia) - Olive groves stretching to horizon - Whitewashed towns on hillsides


Recommended Approach
Option A: Direct to Brindisi (Simple) - Morning Frecce train from Naples - Arrive Brindisi early afternoon (~5.5 hours) - Meet tour group or check into hotel - One journey, minimal hassle
Option B: Stop in Bari (Recommended if Time Allows) - Take morning train to Bari (3.5h) - Spend afternoon/evening in Bari Vecchia (old town) - Watch orecchiette ladies making pasta - Visit Basilica di San Nicola - Fresh seafood dinner along the port - Next morning: Easy 1-1.5 hour regional train to Brindisi
Bari Benefits: - Breaks up long journey - Taste of Puglia before tour begins - Beautiful old town (Bari Vecchia) - Day trip options: Matera (cave dwellings, 1h), Alberobello (trulli houses, 1.5h), Polignano a Mare (cliffs, 30 min)

title: Train Travel in Italy
text:
General Train Travel Tips

Booking Strategy
When to Book: - High-speed trains: 2-4 weeks ahead for Super Economy fares - Regional trains: Can buy same day (no reservations)
Where to Book: - Trenitalia.com or Italotreno.it (direct booking best) - Omio, Rail Europe (third-party, often higher fees) - Station ticket windows (if you prefer in-person)


At the Station
Arrival Time: - High-speed trains: Arrive 15-20 minutes early - Regional trains: Arrive 10 minutes early - Check platform (binario) on departure boards
Validating Tickets: - E-tickets (QR code): No validation needed, show on phone - Paper tickets: MUST validate in yellow machines before boarding - Failure to validate = fine from conductor


On the Train
Luggage: - Store large bags in designated racks (near doors or overhead) - Keep valuables with you - Watch bags during stops
Seats: - High-speed: Assigned seats (on ticket) - Regional: Open seating (first-come, first-served)
Quiet Cars: - Some trains have “Silenzio” cars (no phone calls, quiet conversations)


Train Classes Compared
Trenitalia Classes: - Standard/2nd Class: Comfortable, affordable - Premium: More space, quieter - Business: Leather seats, welcome drink, snacks - Executive: Most spacious, full meal service (rare on our routes)
Italo Classes: - Smart: Economy - Comfort: Business equivalent - Prima: First class equivalent

title: Restaurant Recommendations
text:
General Italy Dining Tips

Meal Structure
Italian meals have courses: 1. Antipasto - Appetizer 2. Primo - First course (pasta, risotto, soup) 3. Secondo - Second course (meat or fish) 4. Contorno - Side vegetable (ordered separately) 5. Dolce - Dessert 6. Caffè - Espresso
You don’t have to order everything! Common to order: - Primo + contorno - OR Secondo + contorno - OR Antipasto + primo


Ordering
Cover Charge (Coperto): €1-3 per person, for bread and table service Service Charge: Sometimes included (servizio incluso) - check bill Water: Ask for “acqua naturale” (still) or “frizzante” (sparkling) Wine: House wine (vino della casa) often excellent and cheap


Tipping

Not expected like in U.S.
Round up bill or leave 5-10% for excellent service
Never 15-20%



Coffee Culture
Stand at the bar: Cheapest (€1-1.50 for espresso) Sit at table: 2-3x more expensive
Types: - Espresso (caffè) - Standard coffee - Cappuccino - Only acceptable before 11 AM - Caffè macchiato - Espresso with dash of milk - Caffè americano - Espresso with hot water (watered-down to Americans)
Never order: Cappuccino after a meal (Italians will judge)

title: Museums & Attractions
text:
Florence Museums

Uffizi Gallery ⭐ PRIORITY BOOKING
Why Visit: Home to the world’s finest Renaissance art collection
Masterpieces: - Botticelli’s Birth of Venus and Primavera - Leonardo da Vinci’s Annunciation - Michelangelo’s Doni Tondo - Caravaggio’s Medusa - Raphael, Titian, and countless others
Practical Information: - Booking: ESSENTIAL - Book 2-3 months ahead - Website: uffizi.it - Price: €20-€25 (includes temporary exhibitions) - Time Needed: 2.5-4 hours - Best Time: First entry (8:15 AM) or late afternoon - Closed: Mondays
Tips: - Book timed entry slot - Arrive 15 min early with printed confirmation - Start on 2nd floor, work chronologically - Don’t miss Botticelli rooms (10-14) - Café terrace has Duomo views



Galleria dell’Accademia (David) ⭐ PRIORITY BOOKING
Why Visit: Michelangelo’s David statue
Highlights: - David - The iconic 17-foot marble masterpiece - Michelangelo’s Prisoners (unfinished sculptures showing his process) - Plaster models and studies - Musical instrument collection
Practical Information: - Booking: ESSENTIAL - Sells out weeks ahead - Website: galleriaaccademiafirenze.it - Price: €12-€16 - Time Needed: 1-1.5 hours - Best Time: First entry (8:15 AM) to see David with fewer crowds - Closed: Mondays
Tips: - Smaller museum than Uffizi - quicker visit - David is in the Tribune gallery (can’t miss it) - Get there early - crowds gather by mid-morning - Photography allowed (no flash)



Duomo Complex (Cathedral, Dome, Baptistery, Bell Tower)
What’s Included: - Cathedral (free entry to nave) - Brunelleschi’s Dome climb - Giotto’s Bell Tower (Campanile) - Baptistery (Ghiberti’s “Gates of Paradise”) - Opera Museum - Crypt
Booking: - Dome Climb: MUST BOOK - Limited capacity, timed entry - Website: duomo.firenze.it - Price: €30 (combo ticket for all sites, valid 3 days) - Dome Climb: 463 steps, no elevator, narrow passages - Time: 2-3 hours for all sites - Closed: Sundays (religious services)
Dome Climb Tips: - Book earliest available time - Not for claustrophobic or mobility-limited - Incredible 360° Florence views from top - See Vasari’s frescoes up close



Bargello Museum
Why Visit: World’s best Renaissance sculpture collection
Highlights: - Donatello’s bronze David (first nude sculpture since antiquity) - Michelangelo’s early works - Della Robbia ceramics - Verrocchio sculptures
Practical Information: - Booking: Recommended but not always essential - Website: bargellomusei.beniculturali.it - Price: €9-€11 - Time Needed: 1.5-2 hours - Best Time: Afternoons (less crowded) - Closed: 2nd and 4th Mondays
Tips: - Often overlooked - fewer crowds - Start on ground floor, work up - Don’t miss Donatello room (first floor)



Medici Chapels
Why Visit: Michelangelo’s sculptural tombs for the Medici family
Highlights: - Tomb of Lorenzo de’ Medici with Dawn and Dusk - Tomb of Giuliano de’ Medici with Day and Night - Cappella dei Principi (Chapel of Princes) - opulent marble - Medici family tombs
Practical Information: - Booking: Recommended - Website: bargellomusei.beniculturali.it - Price: €9 - Time Needed: 45-60 minutes - Closed: Mondays



Palazzo Pitti & Boboli Gardens
What’s Included: - Palatine Gallery (Raphael, Titian paintings) - Royal Apartments - Modern Art Gallery - Costume Gallery - Boboli Gardens (16th-century formal gardens)
Practical Information: - Booking: Recommended for peak times - Website: uffizi.it - Price: €16 (palace + gardens) - Time Needed: 2-3 hours (more if leisurely garden stroll) - Best Time: Morning for palace, afternoon for gardens
Tips: - Gardens are extensive - wear comfortable shoes - Great escape from museum crowds - Café in gardens for break



Santa Croce
Why Visit: Franciscan church with tombs of famous Florentines
Highlights: - Tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli, Rossini - Giotto frescoes (Bardi and Peruzzi Chapels) - Pazzi Chapel by Brunelleschi - Leather school (free to enter from side)
Practical Information: - Booking: Not required - Price: €8 - Time Needed: 45-60 minutes - Dress Code: Shoulders and knees covered



Firenze Card
What Is It: €85 pass valid 72 hours
Includes: - Uffizi, Accademia, Palazzo Pitti, Bargello, Medici Chapels - 60+ museums and sites - Skip-the-line access (reserve time slots)
Worth It? - YES if visiting 4+ major museums in 3 days - NO if leisurely pace (2-3 museums)
Calculate: €20 (Uffizi) + €16 (Accademia) + €16 (Pitti) + €9 (Bargello) = €61 - Card pays for itself with 4 museums - Bonus: Skip lines, flexibility
Buy: firenzecard.it

title: Museums & Attractions
text:
Naples Museums

MANN (Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli) ⭐ PRIORITY
Why Visit: World’s finest Roman artifacts, most from Pompeii & Herculaneum
Collections: - Pompeii and Herculaneum artifacts - Farnese Collection (massive Roman sculptures) - Alexander Mosaic (from Pompeii) - Secret Cabinet (erotic Roman art) - Egyptian collection - Coin and medal collection
Practical Information: - Booking: Recommended (can buy at door but may have lines) - Website: museoarcheologiconapoli.it - Price: €18 - Time Needed: 2-3 hours (could spend full day) - Best Time: Morning - Closed: Tuesdays
Tips: - Go AFTER Herculaneum visit (context makes artifacts meaningful) - Don’t miss Secret Cabinet (room VII) - Huge museum - pace yourself - Café for breaks



Cappella Sansevero ⭐ MUST SEE
Why Visit: The Veiled Christ - one of the world’s most astonishing sculptures
Highlights: - Veiled Christ by Giuseppe Sanmartino (1753) - marble veil appears translucent - Disillusion by Francesco Queirolo - fisherman’s net carved in marble - Modesty by Antonio Corradini - Ceiling fresco Glory of Paradise
Practical Information: - Booking: ESSENTIAL - Timed entry, very small chapel - Website: museosansevero.it - Price: €9 - Time Needed: 30-45 minutes - Photography: NOT allowed - Closed: Tuesdays
Tips: - Book earliest slot available - Tiny chapel - gets very crowded - Stand directly under the Veiled Christ - Worth the booking hassle - unforgettable



Other Naples Sites
Napoli Sotterranea (Underground Naples) - 40 meters below street level - Ancient Roman theater, WWII shelters - Greek aqueducts - Guided tours only - Book at napolisotterranea.org
Castel Nuovo (Maschio Angioino) - Medieval castle - Civic Museum - Great views
Palazzo Reale di Napoli - Royal Palace - Lavish apartments - Throne room

title: Museums & Attractions
text:
General Museum Tips

Booking Strategy
Priority 1 (Book First): 1. Uffizi Gallery 2. Accademia (David) 3. Duomo Dome Climb 4. Cappella Sansevero
Priority 2 (Book Soon After): 5. MANN Naples 6. Palazzo Pitti 7. Bargello 8. Medici Chapels


Timing Your Museum Days
Don’t Over-Schedule: - Max 2 major museums per day - Morning museum + afternoon lighter activity - Build in rest/wandering time
Energy Management: - Start with high-priority museums early in trip - Alternate museum days with outdoor days - Save smaller museums for when fatigued


At the Museum
Arrival: - Arrive 15 minutes early with confirmation - Have ID matching booking name - Print confirmations (don’t rely on phone)
Inside: - Ask for museum map - Identify “must-see” pieces first - Take breaks (museum fatigue is real) - Photography rules vary (usually no flash, sometimes no photos)
Crowds: - Worst: 11 AM - 2 PM - Best: First entry (8:15 AM) or after 4 PM - Avoid weekends if possible

title: Puglia Overview
text:
Puglia at a Glance

Geography
The Heel of the Boot: - 250-mile long region along Adriatic Sea - Mostly flat (unlike mountainous northern Italy) - Endless olive groves (40% of Italy’s olive oil production) - Dramatic limestone coastline - Hot, dry climate (similar to Greece)


History
Ancient Crossroads: - Greek colonies (Magna Graecia, 8th century BC) - Roman conquest and agricultural development - Byzantine influence (Eastern Orthodox traditions) - Norman, Swabian, Spanish rule (Frederick II built Castel del Monte) - Always a bridge between East and West
Result: Unique culture blending Italian, Greek, Byzantine, and Norman influences.


Character
Why It Feels Different: - Less touristy than northern Italy - More Greek/Mediterranean than typically Italian - Rural, agricultural traditions still strong - Slower pace of life - Locals genuinely surprised and pleased to see visitors - Pride in regional identity (Pugliese first, Italian second)

title: Puglia Overview
text:
Expected Tour Highlights
Based on typical Puglia tours, we expect to visit:

Alberobello ⭐ UNESCO World Heritage
The Trulli Capital
What Are Trulli? - Cone-shaped stone buildings unique to Puglia - Built without mortar (dry stone construction) - Whitewashed walls, conical gray stone roofs - Originally built to avoid taxes (could be quickly dismantled when tax collectors came) - Now UNESCO protected
What to See: - Rione Monti (1,000+ trulli, densest concentration) - Rione Aia Piccola (more residential, fewer tourists) - Trullo Sovrano (two-story trullo, now museum) - Church of Sant’Antonio (trullo-style church)
Experience: - Walk through trulli streets - Visit shops in converted trulli - Possible overnight stay IN a trullo - Wine tasting (some trulli are wineries)


Lecce ⭐ “Florence of the South”
Baroque Masterpiece
Why It’s Special: - 17th-century baroque architecture in golden limestone - Incredibly ornate churches and palaces - Compact, walkable historic center - Less crowded than Florence but equally beautiful
What to See: - Piazza del Duomo - One of Italy’s most beautiful squares - Basilica di Santa Croce - Baroque facade covered in sculptures - Roman Amphitheater - 2nd century AD, still partially excavated - Castello Carlo V - 16th-century fortress - Artisan workshops (papier-mâché, ceramics)
Experience: - Baroque architecture walking tour - Pasticciotto (custard-filled pastry) at Caffè Alvino - Evening passeggiata (stroll) in piazzas


Polignano a Mare ⭐ Coastal Drama
Cliffside Beauty
Setting: - Town perched on 20-meter limestone cliffs - Dramatic views over Adriatic Sea - Sea caves below - Former fishing village, now charming resort town
What to See: - Historic Center - Narrow streets, whitewashed buildings - Lama Monachile Beach - Dramatic beach between cliffs - Red Bull Cliff Diving - Location of annual competition - Grotta Palazzese - Restaurant inside sea cave (very expensive)
Experience: - Cliff-top walk with sea views - Swimming (if weather permits) - Seafood lunch overlooking Adriatic - Gelato in historic center


Ostuni - “La Città Bianca” (The White City)
Hilltop Marvel
Appearance: - Whitewashed buildings cascading down hillside - Labyrinth of narrow streets and staircases - Cathedral at the summit - Surrounded by olive groves stretching to sea
What to See: - Historic Center - Explore maze of white streets - Cathedral of Ostuni - Gothic-Romanesque facade - Panoramic Views - Over olive groves to Adriatic - Medieval Walls - Partially intact defensive walls
Experience: - Getting lost in the white maze (intentionally!) - Olive oil tasting - Photography (stunning at any time of day) - Aperitivo with a view


Other Possible Stops
Tours often include some of these:
Matera (Technically Basilicata, but often included) - Sassi di Matera - Ancient cave dwellings, UNESCO site - Continuously inhabited for 9,000 years - Used in films (The Passion of the Christ, No Time to Die)
Castel del Monte ⭐ UNESCO - Frederick II’s mysterious octagonal castle (1240) - Perfect mathematical proportions - Isolated hilltop location - Unknown original purpose
Otranto - Easternmost town in Italy - Byzantine mosaics in cathedral - Turquoise Adriatic waters - Albania visible on clear days
Locorotondo - Circular hilltop town - White houses, narrow streets - Valle d’Itria views
Monopoli - Fishing port with old town - Less touristy than Polignano - Authentic harbor life
Coastal Areas - Beaches along Adriatic coast - Sea caves and grottoes - Swimming opportunities

Regional Specialties
Pasta: - Orecchiette - “Little ears” shaped pasta (Puglia’s signature) - Orecchiette con cime di rapa (with turnip greens, garlic, anchovies) - Cavatelli with tomato sauce
Seafood: - Fresh from Adriatic daily - Grilled fish, octopus, mussels - Sea urchin (ricci di mare) - Riso, patate e cozze (rice, potatoes, mussels - baked)

Wine
Puglia = Italy’s Wine Cellar (produces more wine than any other region)
Red Wines: - Primitivo - Full-bodied, fruity (related to California Zinfandel) - Negroamaro - “Black bitter,” smooth, cherry notes - Primitivo di Manduria - DOC designation, premium - Salice Salentino - Blend, very drinkable

What to Know: - Ancient olive trees (some 1,000+ years old) - DOP designations (Terra di Bari, Dauno, etc.) - Tastings often included in tours - Buy bottles to bring home (pack carefully!)

title: Florence Overview
text:
Florence at a Glance

The Renaissance Happened Here
1400-1600: Florence exploded with artistic and intellectual genius, producing: - Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, Botticelli, Raphael (artists) - Dante, Machiavelli, Galileo (writers, thinkers) - The Medici family (patrons who funded it all) - Brunelleschi’s architectural innovations - Linear perspective, humanist philosophy, modern science
Result: The Renaissance spread from Florence to transform Europe and, eventually, the world.


The Medici Family
Why They Matter: For 300 years (1434-1737), this banking family ruled Florence and bankrolled the Renaissance.
What They Left: - Funded construction of the Duomo’s dome - Commissioned countless masterpieces - Built Palazzo Pitti, Palazzo Vecchio - Established the Uffizi Gallery - Patronized Michelangelo, Leonardo, Botticelli - Founded the Medici Chapels (their mausoleum)
Without the Medici: No Sistine Chapel ceiling (they commissioned Michelangelo), no Birth of Venus, no David statue.

title: Semolina Flours for Orecchiette
text:
Spelling first, because food deserves that much respect: the pasta is orecchiette — “little ears” — not orchietti. This companion note belongs beside the Courgette Zucchini Cream Sauce recipe because the sauce is only half the lesson. The other half is the flour.
The flour in the cooking-class discussion was La Molisana Semola Rimacinata di Grano Italiano: re-milled Italian durum-wheat semolina. This is not the coarse yellow semolina that often turns up in U.S. supermarkets. It is a much finer durum flour, used across southern Italy for fresh pasta, orecchiette, cavatelli, focaccia, and some breads.
For handmade Pugliese pasta, the useful target is therefore semola rimacinata — finely re-milled durum wheat. If the flour is too coarse, the dough can feel gritty and reluctant. If it is too soft and wheat-flour-like, it may lose the firm chew that makes orecchiette worth the trouble.

title: Semolina Flours for Orecchiette
text:
Best U.S. Substitutes

1. Caputo Semola Rimacinata
This is the cleanest match: imported Italian semola rimacinata, fine enough for fresh pasta and close to the flour used in Puglia. If the goal is to reproduce the class as closely as possible, buy this first and stop fussing.


2. Central Milling Organic Fine Durum Flour
A strong specialty alternative. It is very finely milled and therefore much closer to Italian rimacinata than ordinary coarse semolina. Good choice when ordering flour online or when buying from a serious baking/pasta supplier.


3. King Arthur Semolina Flour
A workable, accessible option. It is generally finer than some supermarket semolina flours and useful for pasta and bread, though it is not quite the same thing as Italian semola rimacinata.


4. Bob’s Red Mill Semolina Flour
Common and usable, but usually a little coarser than the Italian flour. It can still make pasta, but the dough may need a little extra water and a little patience. These are not moral failings, merely consequences.

title: Semolina Flours for Orecchiette
text:
Practical Ranking for Orecchiette
For trying to reproduce the Puglia cooking-class pasta at home, use this order:

Caputo Semola Rimacinata — best match.
Central Milling Organic Fine Durum Flour — excellent fine-durum alternative.
King Arthur Semolina Flour — good practical substitute.
Bob’s Red Mill Semolina Flour — acceptable, but coarser; adjust water as needed.

title: Semolina Flours for Orecchiette
text:
Kitchen Notes

Look for the words semola rimacinata or fine durum flour.
Avoid assuming that every bag labeled “semolina” has the same texture. It does not.
If the dough feels dry, sandy, or unwilling to come together, add water gradually rather than dumping it in like a barbarian.
If using a coarser U.S. semolina, expect to knead a little longer and hydrate a little more.
For orecchiette, the flour should help produce a firm, resilient dough that can be dragged, cupped, and turned without collapsing into paste.

title: Final Group Dinner in Putignano
text:
After Matera, the last full night came back to Putignano for the group dinner at Osteria Botteghe Antiche, Piazza Plebiscito 8. The piazza is the heart of old town, with a few bars and restaurants directly in it, and San Pietro Apostolo nearby — considered the main church of Putignano. The original church dated to around the year 1000, but by the fifteenth century it had become too old, too dilapidated, and too small for the town’s needs. In 1477, it was rebuilt by Balì Carafa, the local ruler from the Knights of Jerusalem, later the Knights of Malta.
The order’s name carries a great deal of medieval geography in a small phrase. The Knights Hospitaller began as the Order of St. John in Jerusalem, built around a hospital for pilgrims and recognized by Pope Paschal II in 1113. After the Crusader states fell, the order shifted its base westward: first through Cyprus and Rhodes, and then to Malta in the sixteenth century. So “Knights of Jerusalem” and “Knights of Malta” are not two unrelated groups, but different historical names for the same long-lived Catholic military-hospitaller order as its center of gravity moved across the Mediterranean.
That gave the square more weight than a pleasant dinner setting alone would have done. Piazza Plebiscito was not just a convenient place to eat; it was the old town’s center of gravity, with the church, the bars, the restaurants, and the Friday-night life all gathered together. The square was full of people and families, warm, lively, and inviting: a truly marvelous place for the last night of the trip.
Our own lodging in Putignano had already been making the same point in a quieter way. The sign read Petrantiche, historical center of Apulie — a very modern metal plaque for a place built into old stone.
Then there was the window inscription: 1702, not as the building’s beginning, but as a marker of when it had been updated. Once that one appeared, others began to show up too. Putignano was not performing oldness for visitors; it was simply old, and the stones kept saying so if one bothered to look.
We ate outside with the group: red-and-white checked tablecloths, wine glasses, the old town around us, and the trip beginning to understand that it was almost over.
The most interesting plate was the one with the fried “balls.” They turned out to be hyacinth bulbs — not meatballs, not croquettes, not some harmless anonymous fritter, but bulbs. This is why one takes notes. Italy can still produce a small culinary ambush after two weeks of evidence.
There was also a bright orange soup or sauce course, served in a broad white bowl with herbs, small crisp bits, and red and green garnish. The exact name can wait for a menu or memory to rescue it; visually, it belongs to the same final-night table.
Dessert was pastry, powdered sugar, and yellow cream: a square layered pastry base with a curled yellow topping, served on a pale plate under the indoor-or-evening restaurant light. A proper sweet ending, and less alarming than the bulbs.
The wine from this dinner is entered separately in the running ledger: Tormaresca Calafuria Salento IGT 2023. The bottle did its archival duty. The hyacinth bulbs did the stranger work of making the meal memorable.

title: Otranto Harbor, Punta Palascia, and Porto Badisco
text:
June 15 now has two posts, because the cathedral plainly overpowered the day and demanded its own chamber. Sensible. The focused cathedral post is here: Otranto Cathedral: Basilica of the Annunciation and the Tree of Life.
This post keeps the rest of the day: Otranto as Adriatic harbor, lunch by the water, and the evening coastal run to Punta Palascia / Cape Otranto and Porto Badisco.
The itinerary had Otranto as an ancient Adriatic port town: Greek Hydrus, Roman port, a place facing the Balkans and Greece, with Albania visible across the water on a clear day. That orientation mattered all day. Otranto does not feel like an endpoint so much as one side of a crossing.

The evening plan added one more coastal turn. At 17:00, the group met in the courtyard for pickup. title: Ostuni, Olive Oil, and Putignano
text:
June 17 begins as a working day-post, to be filled in as the evidence arrives. The route is north through Ostuni, onward to Masseria Rienzo for olive oil and lunch, and then into Putignano for the next base. A sensible plan, provided no one lets aperitivo become a committee meeting.
Ostuni did what Ostuni is supposed to do: white stone, hard sunlight, steep lanes, and views out over the lower country toward the Adriatic. The city’s whiteness is not subtle. It bounces the sun back at you like a civic policy.
There was also a cream-filled pastry at a gas station — proof, if any more were required, that Italy has an unfair advantage in even its utilitarian food infrastructure. The sign in town names the thing properly: pasticciotti tradizionali, Ostuni. A gas-station pasticciotto with crema is still a cream-filled pastry worth remembering, because civilization occasionally appears beside a fuel pump and refuses to apologize.
Then came the proper deep-time argument for the day: a 3,000-year-old olive tree, its trunk twisted, hollowed, and folded back on itself, still carrying a full crown of silver-green leaves. The Romans look recent beside a tree like that. So do most arguments.
After the move came the room in the historic center: a narrow whitewashed lane below the balcony, stone paving underfoot, wires and railings overhead, and a wedge of blue sky between the buildings. The accommodations in Putignano are in buildings more than 1,000 years old. Our driver is from Putignano; his ancestors may have lived in some of these same stone rooms, which is a better check-in fact than any hotel welcome card has managed lately. Apulia does not always announce itself with grand monuments. Sometimes it gives you a quiet street out the window — and a vaulted stone ceiling overhead — and lets the stone do the explaining.
The historic center also has the Seat of the Knights of Malta: pale stone buildings gathered around a small paved square, with outdoor tables, potted trees, and the bright blue sky doing its usual Puglian work. Not a bad way for a medieval military order to leave a footprint.
Dinner was at Premiata Pizzeria, properly announced by a black sign promising a “culinary experience,” and then delivered in the more reliable language of hot crust, cheese, cured meat, red peppers, and a table that had already begun to look lived-in. The walk there through Putignano’s historic center was nearly as good: stone paving underfoot, pale facades on either side, string lights overhead, and the evening sky going deep blue above the tower.

title: Matera: Chiesa del Purgatorio
text:
Matera’s Chiesa del Purgatorio deserves its own post because it announces its subject before you cross the threshold. This is not a church that hides death in a side chapel. It puts skulls, bones, souls, angels, and redemption on the facade, right in the white heat of Via Ridola.
The Italian Wikipedia entry identifies it as a Baroque church on Via Ridola, built between 1725 and 1747 with funding from the Confraternity of Purgatory. The theme is exactly what the name promises: death, time, purification, and the hope of redemption. Subtle it is not. Nor should it be.

title: Matera: Chiesa del Purgatorio
text:
Why a church of Purgatory?
The surprise for us was that this was not just one strange Matera church with a taste for skulls. It belongs to a wider Catholic pattern: purgatorial societies or confraternities devoted to praying for the souls in Purgatory. The point was intercession. The living offered Masses, prayers, charity, and remembrance so that the dead — especially those imagined as poor, abandoned, unnamed, or insufficiently aided — might be helped on the way to heaven.
That means the word “confraternity” matters. This was not, as far as the Matera source says, a single religious order dropping identical churches across Italy. It was a lay devotional and charitable form that flourished especially in the Counter-Reformation and Baroque world. Naples gives the loudest example: Santa Maria delle Anime del Purgatorio ad Arco was attached to a congregation founded in the early seventeenth century to offer daily Masses, sacred functions, and charitable works in suffrage for the souls of Purgatory. Its underground cult of the anime pezzentelle — anonymous “poor souls,” often represented through adopted skulls — shows the same theology in a more intensely Neapolitan key.
Matera’s church is part of that family, but with its own local face. Other Italian examples use related names — Purgatorio, Anime del Purgatorio, Anime Sante, or Santa Maria del Suffragio — in places such as Naples, Ruvo di Puglia, Rome, and L’Aquila. The common thread is not tourism-gothic decoration. It is a whole devotional economy of suffrage: the living remember, pray, fund Masses, and perform charity; the dead remain present as souls still being purified.



The Baroque facade of Chiesa del Purgatorio in Matera rising above Via Ridola in hard midday sun.


From below, the building rises in pale stone curves: a swelling facade, heavy portal, carved scrolls, niches, figures, and a dark doorway set back from the glare. Under a hard blue sky near 90°F, the Baroque drama did not need much help. The weather was already preaching mortality.



A close detail of skull carvings beside the entrance steps of Chiesa del Purgatorio.


The skulls are the bluntest sermon. A worn stone post by the entrance carries carved skulls and small relief panels, the memento mori language of the whole church reduced to something you pass at knee height on the way in. Baroque theology sometimes reaches for clouds and angels; here it also grabs you by the ankle.



Visitors standing before the ornate portal of Chiesa del Purgatorio in Matera.


The portal is framed by carved pilasters and a broken, scrolling pediment crowded with figures and inscriptions. Even with tour groups passing through the square, the entrance keeps its force: a public doorway into a church built around purgation, intercession, and the uneasy arithmetic of death and mercy.



The entrance and lower facade of Chiesa del Purgatorio with visitors gathering in the heat.


The facade’s decorations make the subject visible before any guide explains it. Wikipedia notes skulls above the facade and skulls represented in the wooden portal. The effect is a whole exterior program about the caducity of time — the Baroque’s elegant way of saying that time eats everyone, even in a beautiful square.



Chiesa del Purgatorio on Via Ridola, with pedestrians crossing the hot sunlit street.


Stepping back, the church sits firmly in the daily life of Matera: people crossing the street, festival-light frames nearby, the side niche and facade carvings catching the sun. That ordinary street life is part of the force. The church does not set mortality apart from the city; it carves it into the wall everyone walks past.

After the Baroque stonework had done its best to exhaust the eye, lunch was at Giardino Segreto, on Via Principi di Savoia. Sensibly enough, Lecce then supplied food, wine, shade, and the necessary evidence that civilization sometimes arrives on a white rectangular plate.

By evening the day had moved from Baroque stone and lunch plates to the water: the harbor under a bruised blue sky, with the sunset doing its orange work along the horizon.
Lecce also has the remains of its Roman amphitheatre sitting in the open city, half ruin and half civic interruption. Stone seating curves down toward the arena floor while modern buildings, a tall tower, and the ornate Sedile frame the excavation. It is the old Roman habit: leave something large enough in the ground that later centuries must plan their lunch walks around it.

text:
This is the courgette sauce from the June 18 cooking class / food experience: grated courgette gently stewed with onion, blended with mint and cheese, and then folded through pasta. The recipe is short, but it has one command worth treating as law: stew, do not fry.
For the pasta-flour side of the lesson, see the companion note: Semolina Flours for Orecchiette.

text:
Ingredients
For 4 people:

1 large courgette / zucchini, grated
1 onion; the source notes that shallot is better
10 mint leaves
2 tablespoons savory goat ricotta, Parmigiano, or Pecorino Romano
Extra-virgin olive oil
Salt, quanto basta / as needed
Black pepper, if needed

text:

Grater
Bowl
Chef’s knife
Large pan
Blender

title: Courgette Zucchini Cream Sauce
text:
Preparation
Finely chop the onion or shallot.
In a large pan, add 2 tablespoons olive oil and the chopped onion. Stew gently over a low flame, adding 2 tablespoons water.
When the water is more or less absorbed, add the grated courgette. Let it stew for about 3 minutes, uncovered, over low heat.

Pay attention: only stew, do not fry.

When the courgette is cooked, let it cool down.
In a large bowl, combine the stewed courgette, mint leaves, and a pinch of salt. Blend. Add 2 tablespoons grated cheese — savory goat ricotta, Parmigiano, or Pecorino Romano. If necessary, add a little more olive oil and black pepper.
When the pasta is ready, mix the sauce and pasta together in a large bowl.

title: Courgette Zucchini Cream Sauce
text:
Notes

The sauce depends on gentleness: low flame, a little water, and no browning.
Mint keeps the sauce from becoming merely creamy; do not omit it unless you enjoy making food dull on purpose.
The cheese choice changes the character: goat ricotta for tang and softness, Parmigiano for roundness, Pecorino Romano for salt and bite.

title: Alberobello Lunch and Chocolate Salami
text:
June 18 is the Alberobello day: out from Petrantiche Albergo Diffuso in Putignano after breakfast, into the trulli district for the morning, and then lunch on our own in Alberobello before returning to Putignano to cool down and gather strength for the evening food experience.
The morning tour was the trulli doing what trulli do best: whitewashed walls, dry-stone conical roofs, pale paving, hard blue sky, and roof symbols painted in white as if the town had decided ordinary architecture was insufficiently theatrical. A small white Fiat parked among the cones looked less like transportation than a prop left there by a competent stage manager.
From above, Alberobello becomes a whole field of stone cones: white walls below, stacked gray roof courses above, the streets threading between them, and small birds cutting across the sky. The closer rooftop view shows the less polished working edges as well — pots gathered in a courtyard, a rusting corrugated roof, clipped greenery, and the trulli roofs still rising behind it all. That is often the better proof: the famous form not as postcard, but as neighborhood.
The descent back toward the district narrowed the view into stone steps, high walls, deep shade, and a bright opening below where the trulli start again. Three people on the stairway give the scene its scale: the architecture is not just quaint; it channels you downhill like water.
Lunch supplied an important dessert note: chocolate salami. This is not salami, which would make it a poor dessert and a suspicious sausage. It is the chocolate-and-biscuit log sliced to look like salami, a trick that Italy has decided is entirely reasonable. On this point Italy is correct.
The lunch wines are already in the running bottle ledger — Varvaglione IDEA Rosa di Primitivo and Coppi Senatore Primitivo Gioia del Colle 2017 — because wines belong in the wine post, not scattered around like crumbs after dessert.
Dinner moved the day back to Scinuà, Via Santa Lucia 18, in Putignano. The two of us went there for contemporary Apulian cuisine after making pasta during the cooking class and lunch earlier in the day, which is either excellent thematic continuity or a refusal to learn moderation. We both had pasta.
First came a small peach and red onion salad with croutons and a little finely chopped thyme — a compact, bright thing in a glass, and a useful reminder that even the small courses here were not just filler.
One pasta looked like rigatoni — round tubular noodles — though it had a different name. The sauce was a light cream with zucchini and squash or zucchini blossoms, green and generous under flowers, herbs, croutons, and crisp red pieces. The other pasta was orecchiette, with a braised tomato sauce and what seemed like spare rib meat. After a day that had already involved making pasta, this was not restraint. It was research.

title: Naples Walking Tour and Underground
text:
The Naples walking tour began and ended at Fontana del Nettuno, with Toledo folded into the route and the historic center doing what Naples does: narrow streets, crowds, vendors, people, artists, noise, and movement in every direction. It was the sort of city walk where the streets themselves seem to be talking over the guide.
A major stop was the Cathedral of San Gennaro, Naples’ patron saint, who protects the city from disaster — with volcanic eruption always one of the great ever-present possibilities here. From there the tour moved through layers of the city above and below ground: present-day Naples on the surface, ancient Naples underneath.
Along the way Dan and Jane took the Metro, entering through one of the newest and most artistic subway stations in the world, with incredible tile work and extensive new mosaics everywhere. The subway itself was nothing like Japan: far fewer people, trains not packed, and no sense of being carried along by a human river. Naples may be chaotic above ground, but the Metro was surprisingly uncrowded.
The underground portion was an archaeological tour through the ancient street plan: the cardo, the north-south avenues, and the decumanus, the east-west streets, forming the old grid of the city. It was another version of Naples’ central fact: every modern street seems to have another city underneath it, still organizing the life above.
After the tour and lunch, they returned to the Gallerie d’Italia on Toledo to see Caravaggio’s Martyrdom of Saint Ursula and Artemisia Gentileschi’s Samson and Delilah. The day also covered the major surface landmarks — the castle, the opera house, and Galleria Umberto I — enough to feel that they had hit the highlights of Naples.
Dinner finished the day well: Trattoria da Patrizia on the marina, a lovely evening by the water with swordfish, grilled shrimp, and gnocchi with mussels in tomato sauce. Afterward, Naples granted one small practical victory: Dan and Jane were actually able to hail a taxi the old-fashioned way for the trip back to Casa Wenner Large — Naples Center Chiaia Plebiscito, rather than submitting to another round of app-mediated nonsense. A civilized end to a loud, layered, very Neapolitan day.

text:
The day began pleasantly and practically: coffee, quiche, and packing in Florence before the train south. It was not a museum morning or a forced march through another checklist, just the civilized work of closing one chapter of the trip and getting the bags ready for the next.
The Italo ride to Naples was in the club car / private Salotto cabin, a three-hour pocket of calm for the trip south. It turned out to be the last quiet for a while. After Florence’s composed stone and proportion, Naples announced itself with noise, speed, density, and hills: traffic moving through narrow streets at high speed and with rules that were not obvious to outsiders, climbing and dropping everywhere.
A car brought Dan and Jane from Napoli Centrale to Casa Wenner Large — Naples Center Chiaia Plebiscito, the Airbnb on Via Monte di Dio. The apartment is pretty great: quiet, with its own enclosed courtyard, a rustic garden, and a view over the Gulf of Naples. The plants here are tropical and big, which makes the enclosed garden feel more southern immediately — a different climate and a different city, not merely the next stop on the same itinerary.
Dinner was at 10 Diego Vitagliano, Diego Vitagliano’s flagship pizzeria. The “10” is a nod to Diego Maradona’s jersey number — Maradona being nearly a patron saint in Naples — and also to the shared first name. It was a good first Naples dinner in exactly the right category: pizza, serious pizza, and outstanding. The focused pizza note is now here: Pizza at 10 Diego Vitagliano.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text: We spent June 9 sweeping across Florence’s centuries: Renaissance painting and sculpture in the morning, modern color fields in the afternoon, and the practical business of leaving the city in the evening.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Uffizi: The Medici Collection
We began the day at the Uffizi with a private tour in English focused on the Medici collection. Our guide used the rooms as a visual history lesson in the transition from medieval art to the Renaissance — religious forms, human bodies, space, perspective, patronage, and civic ambition all changing at once. Without context the Uffizi can become a long procession of gold halos and crowded rooms; with context, the shift in Western art becomes visible wall by wall.
The highlights included paintings by Botticelli, Michelangelo, and Leonardo da Vinci, along with sculpture connected to Donatello. What struck us most was not only the list of famous names, though the list was formidable. It was the sense of Florence as a workshop of transition, with the Medici collection serving as both treasury and argument.



From the upper floor of the Uffizi, looking west over the Arno toward the Ponte Vecchio.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Accademia: Prisoners and David
From there we continued to the Accademia. The Medici musical instrument collection made a quieter counterpoint to the morning’s paintings — another reminder that Renaissance patronage was not confined to canvas and marble. Then came Michelangelo’s unfinished Prisoners and finally David.
The Prisoners matter because they show the struggle still inside the stone: figures half-emerged, half-captive. Then David stands at the end of that argument, fully released, which is a rather good trick for a block of marble and a young sculptor with dangerous confidence.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Afternoon: Gelato, Errands, Rothko
We turned the afternoon practical: a walk through Florence for last-minute business, with a gelato snack folded in because there are civilized ways to run errands and barbarous ways, and Florence rewards the civilized.
From there, we headed to Palazzo Strozzi for the Mark Rothko exhibition — a sharp change of register after the morning’s Renaissance density. Fewer saints and patrons, more color, silence, and the modern problem of standing before a painting until it starts doing something back.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Last Dinner: Del Fagioli
The evening was our last night in Florence, and Del Fagioli was exactly the right final dinner: one of the few remaining family trattorias in the city, small, quiet, and lovely in atmosphere. We had a properly Florentine dinner — Florentine steak, white beans, green beans, roast potatoes with rosemary, and fried squash blossoms — followed by lemon mousse for dessert, and a Tuscan rosé throughout.
Then the less glamorous but necessary rite of packing for the next day’s train to Naples. A good final sequence, all told: Medici splendor, Michelangelo’s stone, Rothko’s color, gelato, a family trattoria dinner, and bags by the door before the road south.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
text:
We got back from Puglia yesterday, and before I lose the thread, I want to write down what I learned about the wine — specifically the rosé, which turned out to be the story of the whole trip.
I knew Puglia had rosé. I didn’t know it had this much rosé, or that it had been doing serious rosé before Provence made it fashionable. The famous Five Roses from Leone de Castris, bottled in 1943, is often cited as Italy’s first commercially important rosato. That’s not a quirky footnote — it tells you something about how deeply rosé is woven into the region’s wine culture.
Here’s what I found worth knowing.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
section: Negroamaro — The One You’ll See Everywhere
text:
Negroamaro — The One You’ll See Everywhere
This is the signature grape for Puglian rosé, and the name is a little misleading — “black and bitter” — because the rosés are vibrant and food-friendly, not harsh. What you get:

Cherry and raspberry fruit
Mediterranean herbs
A slight savory bitterness on the finish
Enough body to actually pair with food

Think Provence rosé with more personality. It’s great with seafood pasta, burrata, grilled octopus, pizza — basically everything you’re going to eat in Puglia.
Look for: Five Roses (Leone de Castris), Salice Salentino Rosato DOC.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
text:
Primitivo — Rich and Fruity
Primitivo is genetically almost identical to Zinfandel, which I didn’t know going in. In rosé form it becomes much fresher than you’d expect — strawberry, watermelon, red cherry, white pepper, with a fuller mouthfeel and slightly higher alcohol than a typical Provence pour.
Think: White Zinfandel’s sophisticated Italian cousin. Works well with charcuterie, grilled pork, tomato dishes. Wines from Manduria tend to be bigger than those from Gioia del Colle.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
section: Susumaniello — The One Worth Seeking Out
text:
Susumaniello — The One Worth Seeking Out
Nearly extinct not long ago, Susumaniello is now one of Puglia’s most exciting grapes. The rosé is pale to medium pink and tastes like red currants, pink grapefruit, rose petals, and a salty sea-breeze minerality. Less heavy than Primitivo, more elegant than Negroamaro.
Think: somewhere between Provence and Etna rosé. Fantastic with shellfish, raw tuna, shrimp risotto.
Look for: Tenute Rubino Susumaniello Rosato.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
text:
Bombino Nero — Light and Floral
The grape of the Castel del Monte Rosato DOC. Bombino Nero gives color quickly without excessive tannin, which makes it ideal for pale, delicate rosés — wild strawberry, peach, white flowers, citrus. Light body, crisp acidity. Think Italian rosé with a touch of Pinot Noir character.
Look for: Rivera Pungirosa.

title: The Rosés of Puglia
section: Nero di Troia — The Structured One
text:
Nero di Troia — The Structured One
Common in northern Puglia. Cranberry, red cherry, herbal notes, mineral finish. These rosés can actually age, and they have more tannic structure than anything else in the category. Think rosé with some of the seriousness of a red wine.

title: Florence at Walking Pace
text:
The first full morning in Florence began properly: out from the Airbnb and across the Ponte Vecchio, letting the city reveal itself at walking pace rather than schedule pace. The morning target was Cappelli Antonio Gatto, the hatmaker, though the shop was not open on this stroll — a small frustration, but hardly a defeat.
Coffee and pastry came at Caffè Bellini, across the street from the Giardino di Boboli. A good Florentine morning needs very little ceremony: a bridge, a café, something sweet, and enough time not to hurry.
Brunch was at Osteria Belguardo, with fried sage, calamari, spinach salad, and peas with prosciutto. That made the morning feel less like sightseeing and more like settling into the rhythm of the place: walk, look, eat well, keep a few possibilities open.
Later, the walk carried through the courtyard of the Uffizi Gallery, past the tower, and into the civic heart of Florence at Palazzo Vecchio. Outside, in Piazza della Signoria, stood the outdoor copy of Michelangelo’s David — the sort of public art that makes a city feel less like a museum and more like a civilization that left its doors open.
That statue also became a family thread: the text exchange with the grandson about David, along with the photos, belongs in the final record of this trip — not lost in the heathen swamp of message history.
Dinner was outdoors by Palazzo Vecchio: pizza, burrata, salad, and rosé. The evening finished in the proper Italian manner, with gelato on the walk back to the Airbnb.

title: The Duomo Complex, Properly Done
text:
The day began with breakfast on Palazzo Vecchio before walking to the Duomo Complex. The tickets were for a 10:30 entrance to Santa Reparata, through the Porta Campanile entrance on the north side. The ticket was precise enough; the line was not. Despite what the entrance instructions said, the line had wrapped halfway around the huge cathedral, which is a fine way for bureaucracy to make theology look orderly by comparison.
Rather than spend the morning standing in that line, the better move was to tour the Baptistery first. The visit was somewhat diminished by the dome refurbishment — less visible than expected — but still worth seeing as part of the complex.
From there, the route continued to the Opera del Duomo Museum, where there was no line. This proved to be one of the morning’s best decisions. The museum holds a remarkable collection: Ghiberti’s original brass doors, Michelangelo’s Pietà, extensive statuary, Donatello’s wooden Mary Magdalene — haunting — and a creepy collection of reliquaries. Some museums try to impress by accumulation; this one does so by putting several centuries of faith, civic pride, craftsmanship, and mortal anxiety in the same building.
After the museum, the route returned to the Santa Reparata entrance for the cathedral. Inside, the dome could be seen from the cathedral proper, and then the visit continued below to the excavated remains of the earlier cathedral layers. The lower level preserved much of the floor of the central portion of the original cathedral, tomb covers, including one connected with the Medici, and the archaeological bones of Florence’s sacred history.
Late afternoon turned from cathedral stone to the river and the Oltrarno. The walk went along the Ponte Vecchio toward the Boboli Gardens, with a stop at Pin Art — Bottega d’Oltrarno for drawing pencils. From there came the return to Cappelli Antonio Gatto, the custom hat shop that had been closed on the earlier attempt. This time the shop was open, and both of us bought hats. Pictures to follow; a hat bought in Florence deserves photographic evidence, if only to silence future barbarians.
The day closed with dinner, a little clothes shopping for Dan, and gelato before calling it a night. A properly Florentine finish: sacred architecture in the morning, artisan shops in the late afternoon, and gelato at the end because civilization occasionally gets something right.

title: We Made It to Florence
text:
After flying all night from Chicago and connecting through Frankfurt, we arrived in Florence right on the planned 6:30 PM local arrival. The long-haul exhaustion was real, but so was the relief of finally being in Italy.
From Florence Airport we took a taxi into the city to the Airbnb at Aurora apartments Piazzetta, Via Por Santa Maria, 8 — a central landing point just steps from the old heart of Florence. Bags down, travel day behind us, the first evening could begin properly.
Dinner was at Mangiafoco Osteria Tartuferia, which turned out to be exactly the right first-night choice: excellent food, an extensive wine list, and the sort of meal that makes arrival feel official. The carbonara was the best carbonara ever; the steak was remarkable. After a night in the air and a day of airport logistics, it was a perfect way to spend the first evening in Florence.

---
title: "Naples Traffic: First Impressions"
subtitle: "A voice recording on the chaos of Neapolitan traffic, scooters, and narrow streets."
date: "2026-07-03"
author: "DJG"
categories: [italy, travel, naples, transportation]
description: "Notes from a short recording made after arriving in Naples, describing the density of traffic, scooter riding habits, and the adjustment period required to tolerate the ride."
---

## Overview

This page is a supplementary write-up of a short voice recording (COL-2026-07-03 12:31:19, roughly 11 seconds of transcribed speech) made shortly after arriving in Naples. The recording captures an immediate, visceral first reaction to Neapolitan traffic — before any of the archaeology, food, or logistics notes from the rest of the trip.

## The Opening Line

The recording opens with a quote from Jane, delivered within the first hundred feet of leaving on the road in Naples:

> "There should be dead people everywhere."

That line frames the whole recording. It was not an exaggeration made in hindsight — it was said in the moment, while the traffic was actually happening around the car.

## Traffic Density

The recording describes Naples traffic as:

- Cars bumper to bumper, side by side
- Sometimes four and five lanes deep, despite this not being how the road is marked
- Scooters weaving in and out between the cars continuously

The combination of packed car lanes and scooters threading through the gaps is what produced the "dead people everywhere" reaction — the expectation, from the passenger seat, that a collision was imminent and unavoidable.

## Scooter Riding Habits

A specific detail singled out in the recording is how many people ride on a single scooter. Rather than one rider alone, the recording describes scooters often carrying:

- One person plus another person, or
- One person plus one child, with another child standing in front of the driver

This detail is presented as part of what made the scene feel chaotic and, in the recording's own word, "insane" — not just the density of vehicles, but the number of people, including children, riding exposed on scooters within that density.

## The Adjustment Period

Both speakers reportedly wondered "what we'd gotten ourselves into" during this initial exposure to the traffic. The recording notes it took about a day before they could keep their eyes open while riding in a cab through it — a concrete, specific detail about the emotional/physical toll of watching the traffic rather than an abstract complaint.

## Beyond the Main Roads: Narrow Streets

The recording draws a distinction between two different traffic environments in Naples:

1. **Wide roads** — crowded, multi-lane, bumper-to-bumper, with scooters weaving through.
2. **Narrow streets** — once off the main roads, the streets narrow considerably, with really tight turns, and still people and scooters everywhere.

So the chaos wasn't confined to one type of road — it changed character (wide and dense vs. narrow and tight) but didn't let up.

## Key Takeaways

- Naples traffic made an immediate, strong impression — strong enough to produce the line "there should be dead people everywhere" within the first hundred feet of driving.
- Wide roads in Naples can run four to five lanes deep in practice, with scooters cutting between cars.
- Scooters frequently carry more than one rider — often a second adult, or a parent with one or two children, including a child standing in front of the driver.
- It took about a day of exposure before it was tolerable to keep watching the road from inside a cab.
- Even away from the crowded main roads, narrow streets with tight turns kept people and scooters in close proximity to traffic.

text:
Morning
After breakfast at the masseria, drivers shuttle the group to Otranto — an ancient town perched on a rocky bluff overlooking the Adriatic Sea. Its roots are the Greek city Hydrus; its coastal position facing the Balkans and Greece runs through its history as a Roman port. UNESCO designated it a “messenger site of peace.”

title: Day 11 — June 15: Otranto
text:
Daily Retrospective
Otranto’s great surprise was the Tree of Life in the cathedral — not a small decorative mosaic, but an entire medieval pavement world of stories, beasts, scripture, and legend underfoot. The cathedral was the day’s clear highlight: the most remarkable mosaic Dan had ever seen, covering the whole floor section by section and still walked on by visitors.
Lunch was in the harbor overlooking the Adriatic: fresh vegetables, sea bream, a light torte, and plenty of fruit. The setting matched the meal — clean, bright, and maritime rather than heavy.
The evening moved back out toward the coast. Everyone met in the courtyard at 17:00 for pickup, then stopped first at Il Faro, the lighthouse at Punta Palascia / Cape Otranto — the easternmost point of Italy — before continuing to Porto Badisco for bar food, drinks, good company, and wide sea views. The return to Masseria dei Monaci was scheduled for 19:30, a compact coastal coda to a day already shaped by Otranto’s cathedral, harbor, and Adriatic edge.



Il Faro at Punta Palascia / Cape Otranto, the easternmost point of Italy, looking out over the Adriatic.

Morning: Coffee and the City Center

Breakfast
Stand at the bar at a neighborhood café — order un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore. Sitting down doubles the price and removes you from the local experience. Cost: €3–5.


San Lorenzo & Mercato Centrale
The San Lorenzo market area (leather goods, scarves, souvenirs) surrounds the Mercato Centrale covered market. The ground floor has butchers, cheese, and produce; the upstairs food court is excellent for a late-morning snack or early lunch. Lively and genuine.


Piazza della Repubblica
Florence’s main square — built on the old Roman forum grid, with grand 19th-century arcades. Have a coffee at one of the historic cafés (Gilli, Paszkowski) if you want to splurge. Watch the street performers and the Florentine pace.


Piazza della Signoria & the Loggia
The political heart of Renaissance Florence. Donatello’s Judith and Holofernes and Cellini’s Perseus stand in the open-air Loggia dei Lanzi — no ticket, no queue. A copy of Michelangelo’s David stands on the original pedestal in front of Palazzo Vecchio. Walk through slowly.
The Uffizi facade runs along one side. You’ll be inside it on Tuesday, Day 5 — today, just walk past it.

Getting to Your Hotel (~7:00–7:30pm)
Option A: Taxi (Recommended) - Official taxi stand immediately outside arrivals - Fixed fare to city center: €22–25 - ~20 minutes to most Florence hotels - No app needed — just queue at the white taxis
Option B: Tram (T2 Line) - Florence’s new airport tram (T2) connects FLR to the city center - Cost: ~€1.50, every 8–10 minutes - ~25 minutes to SMN (Santa Maria Novella station area) - Good option if hotel is near the historic center and you have manageable luggage

Morning: Santa Reparata — Timed Entry (10:30 AM SHARP)






ImportantTimed Entry — Cannot Be Changed



Santa Reparata: 10:30 AM — Porta Campanile entrance
This is a fixed timed ticket that cannot be rescheduled. Arrive by 10:20 AM. Drop any backpacks at luggage storage (Piazza Duomo 38/r) before arriving at the entrance.



What Is Santa Reparata?
The crypt beneath the Duomo floor — the original 4th-century cathedral on which the current Duomo was built. Excavations reveal layer upon layer of Florentine history: Roman remains, the medieval church, Brunelleschi’s tomb.







Element
What to Know




Brunelleschi’s Tomb
The architect who built the Dome is buried here — simple, almost anonymous slab


Roman remains
Sections of Roman-era structure visible in the foundations


Medieval mosaics
Fragments of the original floor, remarkably preserved


Depth of history
Walking over 2,000 years of layers beneath the cathedral floor



Time: Allow 45–60 minutes.

Baptistery of San Giovanni — North Door Entrance
The octagonal baptistery across from the Duomo facade. Lorenzo Ghiberti’s bronze doors (the ones that gave this pass its name) are on the North and East sides.







Door
What It Is




East Doors (Gates of Paradise)
Ghiberti’s masterpiece — Michelangelo called them worthy of paradise. What you see are high-quality reproductions; originals in the museum.


North Doors
Ghiberti’s earlier work — still extraordinary; your pass enters here



Time: 30–45 minutes inside.


Opera del Duomo Museum (Museo dell’Opera)
Piazza del Duomo 9 — the museum housing the actual originals removed from the Duomo exterior for preservation.







Highlight
What to See




Ghiberti’s Gates of Paradise (originals)
The actual bronze panels — extraordinary up close


Michelangelo’s Bandini Pietà
Late Michelangelo, unfinished, raw, extraordinary — carved for his own tomb


Donatello’s Mary Magdalene
Haunting carved wood figure; one of his most powerful works


Luca della Robbia’s Cantoria
Marble choir gallery with children singing and dancing


Arnolfo’s Madonna
13th-century sculpture from the original cathedral facade



Time: 1–1.5 hours. This museum is excellent and undervisited — give it time.

Morning/Day: Herculaneum & Vesuvius Tour
Check your tour confirmation for the exact schedule. A typical Herculaneum + Vesuvius day:
Herculaneum ruins (2–3 hours)
Herculaneum was buried under a 20-meter lava flow when Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD — which preserved far more than Pompeii’s ash burial.







Site
Why It Matters




The Boat Houses
300 skeletons of people who fled to the shore — the most emotionally powerful moment on the site


House of Neptune & Amphitrite
Vivid blue-and-gold mosaics, astonishingly preserved


Casa dei Cervi
Elite villa with original frescoes and garden statues


Thermopolium
Ancient fast-food counter with food residue still identifiable


Wooden structures
Actual original wood — doors, furniture, beams — impossible at Pompeii



Mount Vesuvius (1–1.5 hours)
Drive up the volcano, then hike ~30 minutes to the crater rim. Looking down into the crater and back across the bay to Naples — this is the source of the destruction you just walked through.

Wear sturdy shoes — the path is volcanic gravel
Bring water and layers (wind at the top)
Views of Naples, the bay, and Capri on clear days

Morning: Brindisi on Foot (9 AM–1 PM)
After the intensity of Florence and Naples, Brindisi is refreshingly calm. A working Mediterranean port, not a tourist hotspot — which is exactly the point.

The Waterfront & Historic Center
Start: Coffee at a local bar near the hotel (not a tourist café — ask the hotel where the locals go).
Walk the inner harbor (Seno di Ponente):







Site
What It Is




Colonne Romane
One intact Roman column marking the end of the Appian Way (Via Appia). This is where ancient Rome physically ended — Julius Caesar, Cicero, Virgil all passed through.


Seno di Ponente
The sheltered inner harbor — fishing boats, Mediterranean ferries, unhurried pace


Castello Svevo
Norman-era castle on the harbor; exterior worth seeing


Piazza Vittorio Emanuele
Main square near the waterfront


Corso Garibaldi
Pedestrian main street into centro storico



Walk time: 60–90 minutes, relaxed pace.


Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Brindisi (Optional)

Modest museum with finds from the ancient Greek and Roman city
Free or low cost entry; helpful context for the columns and the port’s 2,500-year history
Located near the waterfront

title: Cardo and Decumanus: The Roman Street Grid
text: Somewhere on this trip, a guide said “turn left at Cardo III” and I nodded like I knew what that meant. I didn’t. Here’s what I looked up later.

title: Cardo and Decumanus: The Roman Street Grid
text:
The Basic Grid
Roman city planners used two types of streets to organize everything:

Cardo — runs north–south. The main one was called the Cardo Maximus.
Decumanus — runs east–west. The main one was the Decumanus Maximus.

Together they form a grid, and their intersection was typically the center of city life — near the forum, the temples, the baths, the shops.
The modern analogy is almost too simple: cardo = avenues (north–south), decumanus = streets (east–west). Once you have that, any Roman city plan starts to make sense.

title: Cardo and Decumanus: The Roman Street Grid
section: Why It Matters When You’re Walking Around
text:
Why It Matters When You’re Walking Around
In a site like Herculaneum, the excavated city is laid out in blocks (insulae) separated by cardines running toward the sea and decumani crossing them. When a guide says “we’re on Cardo IV” or “this is the Decumanus Maximus,” they’re just telling you your coordinates in the Roman grid.
There could be several parallel cardines (the plural is cardines) and several decumani — numbered out from the center. The Cardo Maximus and Decumanus Maximus were the main arteries; everything else was smaller and numbered outward.

title: Cardo and Decumanus: The Roman Street Grid
section: The Center Was Always the Forum
text:
The Center Was Always the Forum
The intersection of the two main streets almost always put you near:

The forum (marketplace, civic center, political hub)
Temples
Public buildings
Shops and baths

If you’re ever disoriented in a Roman ruin, find the forum and you’ve found the center. Everything else radiates from there.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text: June 9 became a clean survey of Florence across centuries: Renaissance painting and sculpture in the morning, modern color fields in the afternoon, and the practical business of leaving the city in the evening.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Uffizi: The Medici Collection
The day began at the Uffizi with a private tour in English focused on the Medici collection. The guide used the rooms as a visual history lesson in the transition from medieval art to the Renaissance — religious forms, human bodies, space, perspective, patronage, and civic ambition all changing at once. Without context the Uffizi can become a long procession of gold halos and crowded rooms; with context, the shift in Western art becomes visible wall by wall.
The highlights included paintings by Botticelli, Michelangelo, and Leonardo da Vinci, along with sculpture connected to Donatello. The force of the morning was not only the list of famous names, though the list was formidable. It was the sense of Florence as a workshop of transition, with the Medici collection serving as both treasury and argument.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Accademia: Prisoners and David
From there the tour continued to the Accademia. The Medici musical instrument collection made a quieter counterpoint to the morning’s paintings — another reminder that Renaissance patronage was not confined to canvas and marble. Then came Michelangelo’s unfinished Prisoners and finally David.
The Prisoners matter because they show the struggle still inside the stone: figures half-emerged, half-captive. Then David stands at the end of that argument, fully released, which is a rather good trick for a block of marble and a young sculptor with dangerous confidence.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Afternoon: Gelato, Errands, Rothko
The afternoon turned practical: a walk through Florence for last-minute business, with a gelato snack folded in because there are civilized ways to run errands and barbarous ways, and Florence rewards the civilized.
From there, Palazzo Strozzi for the Mark Rothko exhibition — a sharp change of register after the morning’s Renaissance density. Fewer saints and patrons, more color, silence, and the modern problem of standing before a painting until it starts doing something back.

title: Florence’s Final Day: Uffizi, Accademia, and Palazzo Strozzi
text:
Last Dinner: Del Fagioli
The evening was the last night in Florence, and Del Fagioli was exactly the right final dinner: one of the few remaining family trattorias in the city, small, quiet, and lovely in atmosphere. Dinner was properly Florentine — Florentine steak, white beans, green beans, roast potatoes with rosemary, and fried squash blossoms — followed by lemon mousse for dessert, and a Tuscan rosé throughout.
Then the less glamorous but necessary rite of packing for the next day’s train to Naples. A good final sequence, all told: Medici splendor, Michelangelo’s stone, Rothko’s color, gelato, a family trattoria dinner, and bags by the door before the road south.

title: Italy Trip 2026
text:
Why Italy? Why These Regions?
Italy offers layers of history that few places can match. Florence gave birth to the Renaissance, preserving centuries of artistic genius in its museums and churches. Naples guards some of the world’s finest archaeological treasures from Pompeii and Herculaneum. And Puglia—Italy’s hidden gem—beckons with its unique trulli houses, baroque architecture, and authentic southern Italian culture largely untouched by mass tourism.
This trip combines three distinct Italian experiences: - Florence: Four days immersed in Renaissance art—Michelangelo’s David, Botticelli’s Birth of Venus, Brunelleschi’s Dome, and countless treasures from humanity’s creative peak - Naples: Two days exploring the archaeological wonders of Herculaneum and the vibrant, chaotic energy of southern Italy’s largest city - Puglia: Six days discovering the lesser-known heel of Italy’s boot, with its whitewashed hill towns, coastal beauty, and distinctive regional character

title: We Made It to Florence
text:
After flying all night from Chicago and connecting through Frankfurt, we arrived in Florence right on the planned 6:30 PM local arrival. The long-haul exhaustion was real, but so was the relief of finally being in Italy.
From Florence Airport we took a taxi into the city to the Airbnb at Aurora apartments Piazzetta, Via Por Santa Maria, 8 — a central landing point just steps from the old heart of Florence. Bags down, travel day behind us, the first evening could begin properly.
Dinner was at Mangiafoco Osteria Tartuferia, which turned out to be exactly the right first-night choice: excellent food, an extensive wine list, and the sort of meal that makes arrival feel official. The carbonara was the best carbonara ever; the steak was remarkable. After a night in the air and a day of airport logistics, it was a perfect way to spend the first evening in Florence.
The next morning the city came in quietly. Warm light through the Airbnb window, a pigeon on the ledge outside, the neighborhood sounds starting up below. After all the airports and transit and logistics, this was the moment Florence actually arrived.



First morning light from the Airbnb window

title: The Duomo Complex, Properly Done
text:
The day began with breakfast on Palazzo Vecchio before walking to the Duomo Complex. The tickets were for a 10:30 entrance to Santa Reparata, through the Porta Campanile entrance on the north side. The ticket was precise enough; the line was not. Despite what the entrance instructions said, the line had wrapped halfway around the huge cathedral, which is a fine way for bureaucracy to make theology look orderly by comparison.
Rather than spend the morning standing in that line, the better move was to tour the Baptistery first. The visit was somewhat diminished by the dome refurbishment — less visible than expected — but still worth seeing as part of the complex.
From there, the route continued to the Opera del Duomo Museum, where there was no line. This proved to be one of the morning’s best decisions. The museum holds a remarkable collection: Ghiberti’s original brass doors, Michelangelo’s Pietà, extensive statuary, Donatello’s wooden Mary Magdalene — haunting — and a creepy collection of reliquaries. Some museums try to impress by accumulation; this one does so by putting several centuries of faith, civic pride, craftsmanship, and mortal anxiety in the same building.
After the museum, the route returned to the Santa Reparata entrance for the cathedral. Inside, the dome could be seen from the cathedral proper, and then the visit continued below to the excavated remains of the earlier cathedral layers. The lower level preserved much of the floor of the central portion of the original cathedral, tomb covers, including one connected with the Medici, and the archaeological bones of Florence’s sacred history.



Inside Florence Cathedral, looking up past the nave and stone arches to the painted dome — proof that the Duomo Complex had, at last, been done properly.


Late afternoon turned from cathedral stone to the river and the Oltrarno. The walk went along the Ponte Vecchio toward the Boboli Gardens, with a stop at Pin Art — Bottega d’Oltrarno for drawing pencils. From there came the return to Cappelli Antonio Gatto, the custom hat shop that had been closed on the earlier attempt. This time the shop was open, and both of us bought hats. Pictures to follow; a hat bought in Florence deserves photographic evidence, if only to silence future barbarians.
The day closed with dinner, a little clothes shopping for Dan, and gelato before calling it a night. A properly Florentine finish: sacred architecture in the morning, artisan shops in the late afternoon, and gelato at the end because civilization occasionally gets something right.

title: Florence at Walking Pace
text:
The first full morning in Florence began properly: out from the Airbnb and across the Ponte Vecchio, letting the city reveal itself at walking pace rather than schedule pace. The morning target was Cappelli Antonio Gatto, the hatmaker, though the shop was not open on this stroll — a small frustration, but hardly a defeat.
Coffee and pastry came at Caffè Bellini, across the street from the Giardino di Boboli. A good Florentine morning needs very little ceremony: a bridge, a café, something sweet, and enough time not to hurry.
Brunch was at Osteria Belguardo, with fried sage, calamari, spinach salad, and peas with prosciutto. That made the morning feel less like sightseeing and more like settling into the rhythm of the place: walk, look, eat well, keep a few possibilities open.
Later, the walk carried through the courtyard of the Uffizi Gallery, past the tower, and into the civic heart of Florence at Palazzo Vecchio. Outside, in Piazza della Signoria, stood the outdoor copy of Michelangelo’s David — the sort of public art that makes a city feel less like a museum and more like a civilization that left its doors open.



Evening in the Uffizi courtyard, where the long stone corridor frames the Palazzo Vecchio tower like Florence arranged itself for the walker’s benefit.


That statue also became a family thread: the text exchange with the grandson about David, along with the photos, belongs in the final record of this trip — not lost in the heathen swamp of message history.
Dinner was outdoors by Palazzo Vecchio: pizza, burrata, salad, and rosé. The evening finished in the proper Italian manner, with gelato on the walk back to the Airbnb.
